title: Equality at home
hookLine: sharing work fairly between women and men
tomorrow: Arjan's family is new and still unpacking. what do you bring?

cards: Sunday lunch at Simran's house. Her aunts are at the stove, rolling, frying, plating. Her uncles are on the couch with the match on, calling for more chai.
Nobody planned it. It's just how the room arranges itself, every time. Simran carries out a tray, sets it down, and says, loud enough to hear over the TV: in the langar, everybody cooks.
The room goes quiet. Then her dad, Harjit, gets up, a little awkward, and picks up a dish towel.

teach.b: Simran wasn't inventing a rule. In Asa di Var, on Ang 473, Guru Nanak looks at how people talked about women and turns it around.
In paraphrase: we are born of woman, we're shaped in woman, we marry woman, and when one woman is gone we seek another. So why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
And in the langar, the free kitchen, the work isn't sorted by who you are: anyone can knead dough, stir the pot, serve, or wash up.
Today's word is that same kitchen, brought home. Now look back over the week, because every day of it stood in this kitchen too. Stand up: Simran named the wrong out loud, peacefully first.
Dignity: say who you are, plainly. Without fear, which isn't the same as without shaking. Wait with the name, a bead at a time.
Accept, then rise, after half a win. And no caste: one light in everyone.

teach.h: EQUAL AT HOME IS ALL SIX.
teach.b: Equal at home is all six, on a Sunday.
Bebe, watching her son dry a plate, laughs so hard she has to sit down.

how: In the gurdwara langar, women and men cook, serve and wash up side by side, and some Sikh families talk about bringing that same sharing of work home.

o: sharing the work at home fairly between women and men
letting each person keep the chores they were raised to do
a rule that only the elders may decide who does what

games.q: the week in one kitchen — tap the pairs.
p: all six days, on a Sunday

s: in the gurdwara langar, only women cook
anyone can knead, stir, serve or wash up; the work isn't sorted by who you are.
Guru Nanak asks why woman is called lesser, when kings are born of her
Asa di Var, Ang 473, in paraphrase.
equality at home means splitting every chore exactly in half
the lesson is about sharing work fairly and seeing it, not a stopwatch.

games.q: you move in with two roommates, and somehow one of them always ends up doing the dishes. going by this week, what fits best?
o: name it out loud, kindly, and pick up a towel yourself.
leave it; if she minded, she'd say something about it.
make a strict chart and fine anyone who misses a turn.
games.why: stand up, peacefully first; then share the work, the way the langar does. Simran named it, and Harjit picked up a towel.

practice: Count on your fingers the people whose unseen work kept your home running this week: who cooked, who cleaned, who remembered, who drove. Say each name quietly and what they did.
When you run out of fingers, notice whose name came up most, and whether you'd ever thanked them.

wordCard.voice: Equality at home. Sharing the work fairly between women and men, the way the langar shares it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhand, woman, in Guru Nanak's lines on Ang 473.

carryVoice: For the week ahead: equal at home, a dish towel in everyone's hands. Seven days, one kitchen, and Bebe still laughing.

sources.ref: Ang 473, Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak ('bhand jammiai bhand nimmiai... so kio manda aakhiai jit jammeh raajaan'), paraphrased
